 Review
 'I Play Rocky' is a 'phony' take on how Sylvester Stallone made a classic
 Sean Burns 
 November 12, 2026 Share Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in “I Play Rocky.” (Courtesy Amazon MGM Studios) Sylvester Stallone spends so much time self-mythologizing it’s a little odd that other filmmakers would want to do it for him, too. Nevertheless, hot on the heels of 2023’s Stallone-produced Netflix documentary “Sly” and his recent, revisionist autobiography “The Steps,” along comes Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” a shamelessly pandering and mostly made-up chronicle of how an unknown actor with a funny name and a speech impediment wrote and starred in an underdog story that became a classic. The gimmick here is that it’s a movie about the making of “Rocky” done in the style of a “Rocky” movie, and not one of the good ones. Timed to draft off the original picture’s semicentennial, it’s a phony, frictionless pile of content paste akin to Paramount Plus’ risible 2022 behind-the-scenes miniseries “The Offer,” in which the studio celebrated the 50th anniversary of “The Godfather” by depicting every artist involved in making the film as a blundering buffoon.
 Stallone’s story is the stuff of Hollywood legend. A down-on-his-luck actor typecast as hoodlums writes a part for himself as a bighearted palooka who gets a million-to-one shot at the title. Despite being so broke he couldn’t afford to feed his dog, the actor-screenwriter turned down life-changing amounts of cash from studio executives who loved the script but wanted a bankable movie star like Charles Bronson or Burt Reynolds in the role. Stallone insisted that only he could play Rocky Balboa, with legendary producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff mortgaging their houses and shooting the movie on a million-dollar shoestring so that Sly could be the star. It’s an inspirational anecdote, but hardly enough to sustain a 128-minute film. If your idea of drama is actor Anthony Ippolito doing a nightclub comic’s Stallone impression while repeating the title “I Play Rocky” as exasperated studio execs shout larger and larger figures at him, I have good news because that’s most of this movie.
 From left: Jay Duplass as John Avildsen, Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone and AnnaSophia Robb as Sasha Czack in “I Play Rocky.” (Courtesy Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios) Hilariously, Ippolito also played Al Pacino in “The Offer.” (Look out, De Niro, you’ll probably be next in a “Fockers” prequel or something.) His Sly mimicry has been earning early raves out of festivals, yet another example of the common confusion between an actor crafting a performance and someone being able to look and sound like a well-known celebrity. This is how we wound up with Rami Malek winning an Oscar for lip-syncing with false teeth. But to be fair to Ippolito, Peter Gamble’s screenplay doesn’t give him much to play. The movie version of Stallone is always right about everything, so the arc of the story is him overcoming a couple of faint tinges of self-doubt and learning to listen to his wife Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb) when she tells him how much smarter, better and stronger he is than everyone else. The filmmakers claim that Stallone had no creative involvement in the picture, yet they still spend the running time waxing his ego.
 Ippolito isn’t really playing Sylvester Stallone, anyway. He’s playing Rocky Balboa. One of the things I’ve always found endearing about Sly is how thickly he lays on his erudition. Obviously insecure about being seen as a musclehead, he likes to jam 50-cent words into 10-cent conversations, giving interviews that read like he’s inhaled a thesaurus. The movie has exactly one scene in which the protagonist actually talks like his real-life counterpart, rambling about his “existentialist phase” and rattling off a list of literary influences, wowing Chartoff and Winkler during their first meeting. But for the rest of the movie he just sounds like Rocky, a gentle, monosyllabic lummox guilelessly ascending to superstardom. What’s missing is the cunning hustle that’s powered Stallone’s 50-year career. The filmmakers show him working as an usher at New York City’s Baronet and Coronet Theatre, but leave out how he used to scalp tickets for sold-out shows and upcharge patrons for better seats in the general admission auditorium. (They also neglect to mention that he got fired for trying it on the theater’s owner, Walter Reade Jr.) The Stallone depicted in the film isn’t nearly that sly.
 Silly, sometimes galling factual inaccuracies abound. This is one of those films for people who like to think that movies are not the result of careful planning and preparation by a large crew of hard-working artists and technicians, but rather things that magically happen by accident in front of a camera on the day of shooting. Charmlessly played by filmmaker Jay Duplass, original “Rocky” director John G. Avildsen is presented as an incompetent hack who stumbles into greatness with no idea what he’s doing. Still, he fares better than United Artists’ head Arthur Krim. One of the savviest and most quality-conscious moguls in cinema history is rechristened here as “Sandy Maddox” and played by Tracy Letts as a blustery imbecile. Director Peter Farrelly stages it all in his usual barn-door broad comedy style, so even stuff that actually happened feels fake. (Earlier this year, Farrelly made a film for Amazon called “Balls Up” starring Mark Wahlberg and Paul Walter Hauser as condom salesmen who invent a prophylactic that covers the testicles. He also won an Oscar for “Green Book.”)
 Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in “I Play Rocky.” (Courtesy Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios) You’d never know from this picture that “Rocky” was mostly shot in Los Angeles and the production only spent five days in Philadelphia, or that the tear-jerking story about Stallone’s dog has been debunked over and over again since he first started telling it. Gamble’s screenplay seems to operate under some bizarre notion that there was no organized labor in Pennsylvania, but since this is an Amazon movie, I suppose they had to have a subplot where unions are the bad guys. The film also takes place in a much happier alternate universe where Sly’s brother Frank Stallone doesn’t exist, though his abusive father Frank Sr. is played by a wildly unconvincing Matt Dillon.
 I can’t help but wonder what the purpose of all this is, watching a cosplay baby food version of a Hollywood story everybody already knows. You could just as easily watch another, much better underdog tale that proves Sylvester Stallone was the only person who could play Rocky Balboa. It’s called “Rocky,” and it’s one of the greatest movies ever made.
 “I Play Rocky” is now in theaters .
